faq.a: Mycobacteria thrive in well‑ventilated alveolar spaces where oxygen tension is high, allowing replication and cavitation.
faq.q: Why does TB affect the respiratory zone more than the conducting zone?

faq.a: Yes; for example, severe pneumonia can cause airway inflammation (conducting) and alveolar consolidation (respiratory).
faq.q: Can a patient have disease in both zones simultaneously?

faq.a: A focused auscultation pattern (stridor vs wheeze vs crackles) combined with pulse oximetry gives clues to the affected zone.
faq.q: What bedside test helps differentiate zone involvement when imaging is unavailable?

exam: A 3‑year‑old with cough and wheeze has normal chest X‑ray – what is the most likely zone of pathology and why? — Conducting zone bronchiolitis; wheeze without infiltrate points to airway narrowing.

A patient with chronic cough, night sweats and upper‑lobe infiltrates on X‑ray – which zone is diseased and what is the next diagnostic step? — Respiratory zone TB; obtain sputum for AFB smear or GeneXpert.

During ward round you hear fine crackles at the bases of a malnourished HIV patient – what does this suggest about the zone and likely cause? — Respiratory zone involvement; consider Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

A farmer presents with sudden dyspnoea after inhaling dust, with inspiratory stridor – which zone is affected and immediate management? — Upper conducting zone obstruction; give humidified oxygen and consider bronchodilator nebulisation.

You have limited access to radiology; a patient with suspected TB shows low SpO₂ and tachypnoea – how do you decide on zone involvement? — Low SpO₂ indicates impaired gas exchange → respiratory zone disease.
Why is peak expiratory flow less useful in lower‑lobe pneumonia? — It mainly reflects large airway obstruction; pneumonia affects the respiratory zone where diffusion, not flow, is impaired.

A child with sickle cell disease develops acute chest syndrome; which lung zone is primarily compromised and what key treatment principle applies? — Respiratory zone alveolar involvement; give broad‑spectrum antibiotics and supportive oxygen.
Explain why bronchodilators are ineffective in alveolar fibrosis. — They act on smooth muscle of conducting airways; fibrosis is in the respiratory zone where there is no smooth muscle to relax.
ai.title: Respiratory Zones of the Lung
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The lung is divided into conducting and respiratory zones that determine airflow and gas exchange. Understanding these zones guides interpretation of symptoms, imaging, and bedside investigations in low‑resource settings.

b: Conducting zone: warm, humid, filter air
sections.p: The airway is split into two functional zones. The conducting zone (nasal cavity to terminal bronchioles) moves air without gas exchange. The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and sacs) is where O₂ enters blood and CO₂ leaves.

b: Obstruction in conducting zone → stridor, wheeze, reduced breath sounds
Disease in respiratory zone → crackles, hypoxaemia, reduced PaO₂
sections.p: Airflow resistance is highest in the medium bronchi; alveolar surface area determines diffusion capacity. In low‑resource hospitals, simple bedside clues (e.g., wheeze vs crackles) help locate pathology to a zone.

b: TB: cavitation in respiratory zone, chronic cough, night sweats
Bronchiolitis: wheeze, hyper‑inflation, often in infants
sections.p: Many tropical diseases affect specific zones: TB and fungal infections target the respiratory zone; bronchiolitis from viral infection or inhaled toxins affect the conducting zone.

t.b: What zone is involved? → Upper lobe infiltrates suggest TB (respiratory zone); peribronchial thickening suggests bronchiolitis (conducting zone).
Is obstruction central or peripheral? → Low peak flow with normal spirometry suggests central airway disease.
Is gas exchange impaired? → Low SpO₂ points to respiratory‑zone pathology.

b: Stridor on inspiration → upper conducting zone obstruction
Wheeze on expiration → lower conducting zone (bronchi) obstruction
Fine crackles at lung bases → alveolar (respiratory zone) fluid or fibrosis
sections.p: When assessing a patient with dyspnoea, map signs to zones to narrow differential.

b: Assuming wheeze always means asthma; it can arise from bronchiolitis in infants.
Attributing hypoxaemia solely to cardiac disease; alveolar disease may be the cause.
sections.p: Confusing zone‑specific signs leads to mis‑diagnosis.
